meta.title: Who really said "Time is Money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Franklin really did write "Remember that Time is Money" in 1748 — but he didn't coin it. The exact phrase was already in print in 1719, 29 years earlier.
meta.ogDescription: Franklin wrote it in 1748 — but didn't coin it. The exact phrase was already in print in The Free-Thinker in 1719, 29 years before.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Franklin wrote it in Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One (1748), where it opens the letter’s first paragraph of practical hints. The line is genuinely his — but the phrase was already in print in 1719, so he used a maxim rather than minted one.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One
1748, in George Fisher’s The American Instructor: or Young Man’s Best Companion

source.excerpt: Remember that Time is Money. He that can earn Ten Shillings a Day by his Labour, and goes abroad, or sits idle one half of that Day, tho’ he spends but Sixpence during his Diversion or Idleness, ought not to reckon That the only Expence; he has really spent or rather thrown away Five Shillings besides.
trail: 1719 — the exact phrase is already in print, anonymously, in the London periodical The Free-Thinker: a shoemaker’s wife who grasps “the intrinsick Value of Time” tells her husband, in vain, that Time is Money. The passage survives in the collected volume III, London, 1723 ↗

1748 — Benjamin Franklin opens Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One with “Remember that Time is Money,” then does the arithmetic: idle away half a ten-shilling day and you are out five shillings, not the sixpence you actually spent. Full text at Wikisource ↗

The maxim did not start with him — Quote Investigator traces it and finds the 1719 printing twenty-nine years ahead of Franklin, plus older proverbs of the same shape. Quote Investigator: Maxim Origin: Time is Money ↗
Wikiquote lists the sentence in its Sourced section for the 1740s, credited to Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One (1748). Wikiquote: Benjamin Franklin ↗
source.excerptNote: That is the 1748 orthography, capitals and all. The posthumous collected Works print the same sentence as “Remember that time is money” — the lower-case version almost everyone quotes today.

source.rightsNote: Advice to a Young Tradesman was first printed in 1748 and Franklin died in 1790, so the essay and the collected Works that carry it are long out of copyright in the United States. The 1719 Free-Thinker passage quoted alongside it is equally in the public domain.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: Benjamin Franklin
author.metaLine: 1706–1790 · Printer, scientist, diplomat and Founding Father
author.bio: Franklin ran a Philadelphia printing house, published Poor Richard’s Almanack for more than twenty years, did the electrical research that made his name, and was a drafter and signer of the Declaration of Independence. He was also candid about borrowing other people’s lines — “Why should I give my Readers bad lines of my own,” he asked, “when good ones of other People’s are so plenty?” Advice to a Young Tradesman is his own composition; the maxim that made it famous was not.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: Franklin wrote the sentence. What he did not do is invent it — and that is the part almost every retelling gets wrong.

items.who: Not Franklin — an anonymous London essayist
items.why: The exact phrase is in The Free-Thinker for 18 May 1719, no. 121, in a story about a shoemaker’s wife who understood the value of time and a husband who never minded how the minutes passed. Quote Investigator found it by exact-phrase search ↗

Quote Investigator cites the Oxford Dictionary of Proverbs for two much earlier cousins in very different phrasing — “the most costly outlay is time,” attributed to Antiphon, and “They saye tyme is precious” from a 1572 Discourse upon Usury. See the citations ↗

The 1748 text capitalises it: “Remember that Time is Money.” The posthumous collected Works print “Remember that time is money,” which is the form that reached us. Both are Franklin; only the typography moved. Compare the Works text ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Franklin really wrote it — Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One, 1748 — but he picked up a phrase already in circulation rather than coining one. Quote Investigator’s full trace ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Franklin was not writing philosophy. Advice to a Young Tradesman is a short letter of practical hints to a young man starting out, and the famous line opens the first of several paragraphs that each begin “Remember.” What follows is arithmetic, not aphorism: earn ten shillings a day, idle away half of it, and you are down five shillings even though you only spent sixpence on the diversion.

That accounting move — putting unworked hours on the books as a cash loss — is why the sentence outlived the pamphlet. Max Weber reached for Franklin’s advice about time and money to illustrate the argument of The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904–05), using it to show that early capitalism was a moral philosophy rather than simple greed. Weber quotes Franklin’s ethical writings directly ↗
detailsBody: Quote Investigator is careful about what the 1719 match proves: the phrase matches exactly because the search was for an exact match. The viewpoint behind it is much older and can be formulated many different ways, so “first exact printing” and “first expression of the idea” are different questions. Quote Investigator, ‘Maxim Origin: Time is Money’ ↗

The passage sits in the collected third volume of The Free-Thinker, printed in London in 1723, which gathers the 1719 numbers from March onward. The scanned copy at the Internet Archive carries it, in an OCR that garbles ‘is’ into ‘it’ but leaves the sentence unmistakable. The Free-Thinker, vol. III (1723) ↗
context.pull: “Remember that Time is Money.” Franklin wrote it — twenty-nine years after somebody else printed it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator confirms Franklin employed the maxim in 1748 in 'Advice to a Young Tradesman', quotes the full passage, and documents the exact phrase 'Time is Money' earlier, in The Free-Thinker, 18 May 1719, no. 121, page 128 (GN page 119), London; it also cites the Oxford Dictionary of Proverbs for 'the most costly outlay is time' (Antiphon) and the 1572 Discourse upon Usury 'They saye tyme is precious.'

The essay text is headed 'ADVICE TO A YOUNG TRADESMAN. WRITTEN ANNO 1748.' and opens 'REMEMBER that time is money. He that can earn ten shillings a day by his labour... he has really spent, or rather thrown away, five shillings besides.'

The scanned collected volume III of The Free-Thinker (London, 1723), which begins with No. 106 of Friday 27 March 1719, contains the passage 'I remember to have heard of a notable Woman, who was thoroughly sensible of the intrinsick Value of Time: Her Husband was a Shoe-maker... In vain did his Wife inculcate to him, That Time is Money' — the OCR renders 'is' as 'it' — on the page immediately preceding issue No. 122 of 1719.

States the phrase was already in print in 1719 in the Whig newspaper The Free-Thinker — 'In vain did his Wife inculcate to him, That Time is Money ...' (citing The Free-Thinker, vol. III, from Lady-day to Michaelmas, 1719, London, 1723, p. 128) — and that Franklin's essay 'Advice to a Young Tradesman' appeared in George Fisher's 1748 book The American Instructor: or Young Man's Best Companion.
Lists 'Remember that time is money.' in the Sourced section, 1740s subsection, credited to Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One (1748).

Reproduces the 1748 wording with original capitalisation: 'Remember that Time is Money. He that can earn Ten Shillings a Day by his Labour, and goes abroad, or sits idle one half of that Day, tho' he spends but Sixpence during his Diversion or Idleness, ought not to reckon That the only Expence; he has really spent or rather thrown away Five Shillings besides.'

Benjamin Franklin (January 17, 1706 – April 17, 1790) was an American polymath, a Founding Father, a drafter and signer of the Declaration of Independence, a printer, publisher of almanacs, diplomat and scientist known for work on electricity.

States 'To illustrate his theory, Weber quotes the ethical writings of Benjamin Franklin' — an extended passage about time and money — used to argue the spirit of capitalism was a moral philosophy rather than mere greed; the work was published 1904–1905, first translated into English by Talcott Parsons in 1930.
